tagline.text: December in Roxas City: a river procession for the Virgin Mary and street dancing

location.label: Location
location.text: Roxas City, Capiz (City Plaza, the cathedral, and the Panay River area)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Early December (around the December 8 feast of the Immaculate Conception)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–6,000 (1 night, 2 days, lodging, meals, and local transport; flights not included)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Roxas Airport (RXS), or Kalibo International Airport (KLO) and Iloilo International Airport (ILO)

children.text: Sinadya sa Halaran is a festival held in Roxas City, Capiz, in early December each year. It combines Masses and a river procession honoring the city's patroness, the Immaculate Conception, with street dancing contests and a food fair. For about a week around the December 8 feast day, the whole city is in a festive mood.

Sinadya sa Halaran is a festival held in early December in Roxas City, the main city of Capiz in the Western Visayas. It peaks on December 8, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, the city's patron saint, and runs for about a week, mixing religious events such as Masses and processions with civic events such as street dancing, concerts, and a food fair. It is not as huge as the Philippines' best-known festivals, but its appeal is that you can see the simple, warm year-end spirit of Roxas City, famous for its seafood, up close.

The name comes from the merging of two festivals. Roxas City's Sinadya ("joy" or "sharing") and the province-wide Halaran ("offering") were once held separately, and they are said to have been combined because holding two big festivals in a single year was too expensive. Many accounts place the merger in the early 1990s, but the year differs from source to source, so it is safer not to state an exact year. These days the city often promotes the event as the Sinadya Festival, while locals still call it Halaran or Sinadya sa Halaran. Local tradition links Halaran to the Maragtas legend of the Bornean datus who crossed to Panay, and one study says older babaylan rituals gave way to Masses and processions. Some sources say Halaran began in 1975, but that also varies by source, so it is not stated as fact here.

The center of the festival is the Immaculate Conception Metropolitan Cathedral next to City Plaza in Roxas City. The cathedral took its present form on top of a stone church built in the 19th century, and Capiz became a diocese in 1951 and an archdiocese in 1976. During the festival the cathedral holds a nine-day novena and Masses, and on the feast day a bishop celebrates Mass and a procession of saints' images moves through the city. Civic events take place at City Plaza, the civic center, and parks toward Baybay Beach.

The scene most travelers remember is the river procession, the Prosesyon sa Suba, on the evening of December 7. A boat carrying the image of the Virgin Mary and boats lit with lights go down the Panay River toward the cathedral, and on the same day the Kasanag, the lighting of the Christmas tree and lanterns, takes place at City Plaza. December 8 follows with a morning Mass, fireworks, and civic events such as street dance contests. The order and timing of events change every year, so check the official schedule.

On the evening of December 7 a boat carrying the image of the Immaculate Conception and boats lit with lights move down the Panay River to the cathedral. It is counted among the most photogenic scenes in the city, so claim a spot by the river early. In 2020 and 2021 the festival was held online, and in-person celebrations resumed from 2022.

blocks.title: Feast Day Mass of the Immaculate Conception

children.text: On December 8 a bishop celebrates a pontifical Mass at the cathedral, and a procession of saints' images goes through downtown. The Mass is an important event for local worshippers, so watch quietly as a visitor and cover your shoulders and knees.

blocks.title: Sinadya sa Kalye (street march and drum contest)

children.text: As in the drum and lyre competition held on the opening day, school bands march through the streets and compete. Drums and horns fill the city, and students come out in colorful uniforms.

Contingents from the cities and towns of Capiz compete in a dance contest with traditional costumes and staged scenes. Many teams are described as taking themes such as rice planting, traditional wedding dances, and seafood. The lineup differs from year to year.
A variety show that presents the traditions and festivals of Capiz through song and dance. It is held at the plaza and draws the largest family audience among the programs.
A parade led by large figures (higantes); the figures are sometimes displayed at the plaza. A good place to take photos with children.
A paddling race that shows the role of the bangka is reported to be held. It reflects the identity of a river and fishing city.
Roxas City styles itself the "Seafood Capital of the Philippines." The nights with the food fair and fireworks at the plaza are when the most local families gather.
Arrive at Roxas Airport, or by bus from Kalibo or Iloilo, and leave your bags at your lodging. During the festival rooms fill up early, so check the check-in time.
Walk around City Plaza and the cathedral, and browse the display of giant figures and the fair.
Have an early dinner at a seafood restaurant. The restaurant strip near Baybay Beach is well known; before ordering, check the price per weight and the cooking fee.
Head to the Panay River bank and claim a spot for the Prosesyon sa Suba.
Return to the plaza to see the Kasanag lighting and the performances.
The next day, quietly attend the feast day Mass at the cathedral, or watch the civic events at the plaza.
Have lunch downtown, then head to the airport or the bus terminal.
Event times change every year. The times above show the general flow as an example, and the official schedule takes priority.

items.title: Day-trip route
items.subtitle: A round trip from Kalibo or Iloilo

children.text: Take a bus or van to Roxas from Kalibo or Iloilo. It is said to take about 2 hours from Kalibo and about 3 hours from Iloilo.
Arrive, have lunch around City Plaza and the cathedral, and look at the fair.
Finish dinner at a seafood restaurant before the evening events and watch the plaza performances.
Check the last departure time and head back.
During the festival, public transport late at night may thin out, so check your ride back first.
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific are known to fly from Manila to Roxas Airport (RXS), taking about
1 hour
. One-way fares vary greatly by season, so book early for the December festival.
The airport is close to downtown, about
10–15 minutes
by tricycle.
The bus or van from Kalibo to Roxas is said to take about
2 hours
, and from Iloilo about
3 hours
. From Iloilo, buses and vans leave frequently from the northern terminal.
From Boracay, go from the Caticlan wharf to Kalibo and transfer to a Roxas-bound ride.
Fares and schedules change every year. Check on the spot.
Tricycles are the most common way to get around town, and City Plaza, the cathedral, and the riverside can be reached on foot.
During events the main roads are blocked, so walking is faster.

The festival is held in early December each year and centers on the December 8 feast of the Immaculate Conception. The recent schedule opened on December 5 and ended with a pontifical Mass on December 8, but earlier years were described as December 3–8 or 4–8, so it varies every year. One group's 2024 program was listed as December 1 to 9.

December is the start of the cool dry season in the Philippines, but some years a tropical depression passes through. The 2025 opening was held under the influence of Tropical Depression Wilma, and some outdoor events were moved indoors. Check the weather forecast and bring a rain jacket.

In December many families come home for the holidays, so lodging fills up early. If you choose a place within walking distance of City Plaza and the cathedral, your route through the events is easier, and it is best to book one or two months ahead together with your flight. Rates can be higher than usual, so check prices before you book.

Roxas City styles itself the seafood capital of the Philippines. You can taste oysters, crab, shrimp, and shellfish dishes around Baybay Beach and at the fair, and prices are said to be lower than in Manila. At a paluto restaurant, where you pick ingredients and have them cooked, always ask about the price per weight and the cooking fee before ordering. Bring plenty of cash.

The festival marks the start of the Philippine Christmas season, so the plaza and streets are full of lanterns and decorations. Local families and students gather at the plaza every evening, so it is polite to ask permission before photographing people. The Virgin Mary procession is an act of faith, so take part quietly in keeping with the local mood rather than behaving like a tourist. The reason to visit this city is the warm local events and seafood meals rather than spectacle, so it is best to keep your schedule loose.
Check the official schedule with Roxas City Hall and the Capiz provincial tourism office before you leave.
Seats along the river for the Prosesyon sa Suba fill up quickly, so arrive an hour before the procession.
Book lodging and flights one or two months ahead if possible.
Inside the cathedral, cover your shoulders and knees and refrain from taking photos during Mass.
Some years a tropical depression passes through, so bring a rain jacket and a waterproof bag.
The plaza is crowded, so keep your wallet and phone in front of you.
After the procession, public transport late at night thins out, so decide how you will get back in advance.
Staying a few more days until Christmas to enjoy downtown Roxas City and its seafood is also a good plan.
As a local event, there may be little foreign-language information. The official notices from Roxas City Hall are the most accurate source for the schedule.
Event dates and order change every year, and depending on the weather outdoor events may be moved indoors or reduced. Always check the official schedule before you leave.
During the festival, lodging, flights, and buses are all crowded and prices can rise.
The riverside and plaza are packed, and pickpockets may be about, so guard your belongings.
Stay quiet during religious events and avoid flash photography during Mass.
At seafood restaurants, do not order items without a listed price, and ask for the total first.
During typhoons and low-pressure periods, low-lying areas around the Panay River can flood, so check weather bulletins.
